'''Antoni Bonifacy Przeborski''' (27 May 1871 – 24 May 1941) was a Polish [[mathematician]].<ref name="PWN">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Przeborski Antoni Bonifacy |encyclopedia=Encyklopedia PWN |url=https://encyklopedia.pwn.pl/haslo/Przeborski-Antoni-Bonifacy;3963154.html |language=pl |access-date=11 June 2026}}</ref> He was a professor at [[Kharkiv University]] in the [[Russian Empire]] and was elected [[rector (academia)|rector]] of that institution. From 1922 until 1939 he occupied the chair of [[theoretical mechanics]] at the [[University of Warsaw]] in the [[Second Polish Republic]].<ref name="MacTutor">{{cite web |title=Creators of the Polish school of mathematics |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Polish_Maths_Creators/ |website=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive |publisher=University of St Andrews |access-date=11 June 2026}}</ref><ref name="PWN" /><ref name="Duda">{{cite journal |last=Duda |first=Roman |title=Emigration of mathematicians from Poland in the 20th century (roughly 1919–1989) |journal=Organon |volume=44 |year=2012 |page=96 |url=https://ihnpan.pl/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/7_duda.pdf}}</ref>

==Education and early career==
Przeborski was born on 27 May 1871 in Chorosza (near Lipovets), which was part of the Russian Empire at the time and is now located in [[Ukraine]].<ref name="PWN" /> After completing his secondary education and earning a gold medal from the gymnasium in [[Mykolaiv|Nikolaev]], where his father worked as a physician for the [[Black Sea Fleet]], he attended the Faculty of Physics and Mathematics at [[Saint Vladimir Imperial University of Kiev|Saint Vladimir University in Kyiv]].<ref name="MacTutor" /> In 1895 he won the Professor I. I. Rachmaninoff Prize for his work titled ''On the methods of Abel, Jacobi, Liouville and Weierstrass in the theory of elliptic functions''.<ref name="MacTutor" /> Additionally, he studied at the universities of Moscow, [[University of Göttingen|Göttingen]] and [[Heidelberg University|Heidelberg]].<ref name="PWN" />

==Kharkiv==
In 1905 Przeborski became a professor at Kharkiv University; in 1908 he became an [[ordinary professor]] of mathematics there. He was elected rector of Kharkiv University, and during the [[Polish–Soviet War]] he was taken into custody by the Soviet authorities as a "Polish hostage".<ref name="MacTutor" /> In August 1921 Przeborski submitted an application to the Polish Ministry of Religious Denominations and Public Education for help obtaining permission to move permanently to Poland.<ref name="MacTutor" />

==Warsaw==
Przeborski was one of the mathematicians who left the former Russian Empire for Poland after the [[Russian Revolution|revolution]].<ref name="Duda" /> In 1921 he was for a short time an ordinary professor at [[Vilnius University|Stefan Batory University]] in [[Vilnius]]; in 1922 he moved to Warsaw with the help of [[Wacław Sierpiński]], where he was elected ordinary professor in the Department of Theoretical Mechanics at the University of Warsaw.<ref name="MacTutor" /> He held the theoretical mechanics chair until 1939.<ref name="PWN" />

Since 1923 he was a member of the [[Polish Academy of Learning]], and since 1930 of the [[Warsaw Scientific Society]].<ref name="PWN" /> Przeborski died in Warsaw on 24 May 1941.<ref name="PWN" />

==Scientific work==
Przeborski's research was done in fields such as analytic and real functions, [[integral equation]]s, [[differential geometry]], and applications of mathematics.<ref name="PWN" /> The research he conducted in Poland was mostly related to [[classical mechanics]].<ref name="MacTutor" />

==Selected works==
* ''Wykłady mechaniki teoretycznej'' [Lectures on Theoretical Mechanics], vols. I–II. Warsaw, 1930–1935.<ref name="PWN" />
